## Setting up the physics

Pick solar salt (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃) — the standard two-tank CSP storage medium — operating 290°C → 555°C (ΔT = 265 K), cp ≈ 1.53 kJ/kg·K, average density ≈ 1,850 kg/m³.

Energy density = cp·ΔT = 1,530 J/kg·K × 265 K = 405 kJ/kg = **112.6 Wh/kg**

For 5 MWh (= 1.8×10¹⁰ J):

**m = 1.8×10¹⁰ / 405,450 ≈ 44.4 tonnes of salt**, volume ≈ 24 m³ (needs ~58 m³ of tank volume once you size *two* tanks, hot + cold, each for the full inventory plus freeboard).

## Building the installed cost bottom-up

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (nitrate blend) | 44.4 t × ~$700/t | $31,000 |
| Tanks ×2 (insulated; hot tank in 347H stainless, cold in C-steel; foundations) | 58 m³ × ~$3,500/m³ | $203,000 |
| Salt-to-process heat exchanger | ~1 MWt duty, corrosion-resistant alloy, fabrication floor cost | $200,000 |
| Salt circulation pumps ×2 | specialty long-shaft cantilever pumps, high fixed engineering cost | $160,000 |
| Electric trace heating (freeze protection, salt freezes ~220°C) | small-system floor cost | $40,000 |
| Hot/cold piping (alloy, insulated) | short runs, still has a fabrication floor | $60,000 |
| Instrumentation & controls | PLC, level/temp/flow, floor cost | $65,000 |
| Electrical/power supply | | $30,000 |
| Site/structural | | $50,000 |
| **Direct equipment/material subtotal** | | **≈ $840,000** |
| + Field installation labor (~40%) | | $335,000 |
| + EPC, engineering, PM, commissioning, contingency (~25%) | | ~$295,000 |
| **Total installed cost** | | **≈ $1.45M** |

**≈ $290/kWh of storage capacity.**

Sanity check: salt alone costs ~$6/kWh, consistent with literature figures for bulk nitrate salt at utility scale (~$5–10/kWh). The other ~98% of cost is pumps, HX, controls, trace heat and EPC — equipment with **fixed cost floors that don't shrink with tank size**. This is the key first-principles finding: molten-salt TES has strong economies of scale (utility CSP plants report $15–40/kWh installed at hundreds-of-MWh scale), and a 5 MWh system pays roughly a **10× small-scale penalty**. Practically, nobody builds two-tank molten salt storage at this size commercially — below ~50 MWh it loses to packed-bed rock, PCM, or hot-water tanks, and well below that it loses to batteries outright.

## Amortized over cycle life

Molten salt TES degrades negligibly per cycle (it's sensible heat, not electrochemistry) — life is set by tank/pump/corrosion fatigue, ~25–30 years, roughly one cycle/day → ~9,000 cycles.

- Delivered energy/cycle ≈ 5,000 kWh × 0.95 (HX + standby-loss derate) ≈ 4,750 kWh
- Lifetime delivered energy ≈ 9,125 cycles × 4,750 kWh ≈ 43 GWh
- Capex-only levelized cost: $1.45M / 43 GWh ≈ **3.3¢/kWh**
- Adding O&M (~2%/yr of capex) and a real discount rate (~7%) pushes this to roughly **8–12¢/kWh delivered** (undiscounted vs. discounted bookends).

## Is it cost-competitive with Li-ion? — depends entirely on what "delivered" means

**As thermal storage (heat in → heat out, e.g. industrial process heat or CSP steam backup):** TES wins decisively. No round-trip electrical conversion is needed, lifespan is 2–3× a Li-ion pack with no augmentation, and at any meaningful scale (>50 MWh) the $/kWh undercuts Li-ion by an order of magnitude. Li-ion isn't really a competitor here — you wouldn't use a battery to make heat.

**As electricity storage (a "Carnot battery": charge via resistive heat/heat pump, discharge via a turbine back to AC):** Li-ion wins clearly at this 5 MWh/1 MW scale. You'd need to add a power block (turbine + generator, ~$1,000–1,500/kW, itself diseconomic below a few MW), and round-trip efficiency collapses to 40–60% (Carnot-limited) vs. Li-ion's 90%+. Effective $/kWh of *electricity* delivered from a small TES-plus-turbine system would likely exceed $1,000–2,000/kWh — well above Li-ion's current $300–600/kWh installed cost at comparable small scale.

**Bottom line:** at 5 MWh, molten-salt TES is roughly $290/kWh installed and ~8–12¢/kWh levelized as *thermal* output — cheap and competitive for heat delivery, but this scale is below where TES is normally economical, and if the real requirement is electricity-in/electricity-out, Li-ion beats it today. TES only overtakes Li-ion economically once you're (a) delivering heat directly, not electricity, and (b) operating at hundred-MWh-plus scale where its fixed costs amortize away.
